title: How agile ways of working support OCM
blurb: Name the six ways agile working helps people adopt change, and match each to the effect it has.
question: A train operator is rolling out a new rostering tool. How do frequent releases, user representation, testing, demos, retrospectives and feedback help staff actually adopt it?

teach.h: Agile is a change-friendly way to deliver
teach.body: Organizational change management is about people moving from the current state to the target state. Agile ways of working help, because they deliver change in small pieces, put users inside the work and listen to them all the time. The PRINCE2 Agile book names six ways agile working supports OCM. Learn each one with the effect it has: that pairing is what the exam checks.

head: Agile way of working
How it helps change land
rows: Learn lessons, act on them to improve adoption
Used during iterations and after a release
teach.caption: Book 4.2.4, paraphrased.

teach.h: One big release versus frequent releases

steps.label:
Build with a
user in the team

teach.body: People adopt what they understand and helped to shape. Frequent releases keep each step small enough to absorb. A user in the delivery team brings the organization's view inside the work. Testing and demos let users see and react to real products early. Retrospectives turn what was learned into improvements, and regular feedback keeps steering the product during iterations and after each release.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.4; PRINCE2 7 manual 3.3 (co-creation)

items.label: One depot views rosters on the new tool
Shift swaps added after driver feedback

teach.caption: Each release is small enough for staff to absorb, and shaped by the last.

teach.body: Brightwell Trains is replacing paper rosters with an app. Chief product owner Aisha Rahman puts train driver Callum Reid in the delivery team as a user representative. Drivers test each increment, and every progress review includes a demo for depot staff. Feedback from the demo shows swaps matter more than leave requests, so the backlog is reprioritized. Retrospectives improve how the team runs demos. By release 3, drivers are asking for the switch rather than resisting it.

teach.text: Retrospectives happen at the end of an iteration. They help the team learn lessons and improve change adoption; they are not a tool for tracking progress during an iteration (burn charts and dashboards do that). And demos belong to progress reviews, where users see working products.

items: Frequent releases: incremental, smooth adoption of change.
User representation in the delivery team: organizational adoption.
Progress reviews with demos: user engagement and faster adoption.
Retrospectives: learn lessons and act on them to improve adoption.
Regular feedback: built in during iterations and after a release.

summary: You can now name the six ways agile working supports OCM and match each to its effect. You can also explain why small releases with users involved make change easier to adopt than one large release.

A.q: Which agile way of working supports OCM by allowing incremental and smooth adoption of change?
options: Retrospectives
Frequent releases
Frequent testing
User representation
A.why: Frequent releases allow for incremental and smooth adoption of change (book 4.2.4).

whyNot.0: Retrospectives help the team learn lessons and improve adoption.
whyNot.3: User representation in the delivery team facilitates organizational adoption.

A.q: How does user representation in the delivery team support OCM?
options: It lets users approve the project's tolerances
It replaces testing by other team members
It removes the need for a product owner
It helps adoption across the organization
A.why: User representation in the delivery team facilitates organizational adoption (book 4.2.4).

whyNot.0: Tolerances are set through governance by the business layer and board.
whyNot.1: Testing still happens and is itself a separate OCM enabler.
whyNot.2: The product owner role remains; a user in the team does not replace it.

A.q: Which agile practice supports OCM by giving chances to learn lessons and act on them to improve change adoption?
options: Retrospectives
Progress reviews with demos
Frequent releases
Daily stand-ups
A.why: Retrospectives provide opportunities to learn lessons and act upon them to improve change adoption (book 4.2.4).

whyNot.1: Progress reviews with demos enable user engagement and faster adoption.
whyNot.2: Frequent releases allow incremental and smooth adoption.
whyNot.3: Stand-ups coordinate daily work; they are not one of the six OCM enablers named.

B.q: Progress reviews that include demos support OCM mainly by:
options: fixing the project's time and cost tolerances
tracking progress within each iteration
replacing the need for user acceptance
enabling user engagement and faster adoption
B.why: Progress reviews, including demos, enable user engagement and improve the speed of adoption (book 4.2.4).

whyNot.0: Time and cost are fixed through governance, not by demos.
whyNot.1: Progress within an iteration is tracked with burn charts and team dashboards.
whyNot.2: Demos gather feedback; acceptance by users still takes place.

B.q:
Which two statements about agile and OCM are correct?
1. Frequent testing increases user engagement.
2. Retrospectives are the main way to track progress during an iteration.
3. Regular feedback can be built in during iterations and after a release.
4. Frequent releases make adoption harder, so they are limited.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
B.why: Frequent testing increases user engagement, and regular feedback can be incorporated during iterations and after a release (book 4.2.4).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: retrospectives happen at the end of an iteration and are for improvement.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: retrospectives do not track progress, and frequent releases ease adoption.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: frequent releases allow incremental, smooth adoption.

B.q: Which is NOT one of the ways agile working supports OCM in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Frequent testing
Regular feedback
User representation in the team
A single release at the end
B.why: The book lists frequent releases, user representation, frequent testing, progress reviews with demos, retrospectives and regular feedback; one release at the end is the opposite of frequent releases.

whyNot.0: Frequent testing is listed: it increases user engagement.
whyNot.1: Regular feedback is listed: it is used during iterations and after releases.
whyNot.2: User representation is listed: it facilitates organizational adoption.

C.q: A team wants users to see working features each iteration and react to them. Which event does this, and what OCM effect does it bring?
options: Team retrospective workshop: user engagement and faster adoption
Progress review with a demo: user engagement and faster adoption
Daily stand-up: adoption across the whole organization
Burn-down chart review: incremental adoption of the change
C.why: Progress reviews, including demos, enable user engagement and improve the speed of adoption (book 4.2.4).

whyNot.0: The right effect, but retrospectives are for the team to learn and improve, not to show users features.
whyNot.2: Stand-ups coordinate the team; organizational adoption comes from user representation.
whyNot.3: A burn-down shows remaining work; incremental adoption comes from frequent releases.

C.q: A sponsor wants every new feature released together at the end 'so staff are not confused'. Why is this weaker for OCM?
options: Frequent releases let staff adopt the change step by step
A late release breaks the zero tolerance for scope
Single releases need approval from project assurance
End-of-project releases skip the managing a stage boundary process
C.why: Frequent releases allow for incremental and smooth adoption of change (book 4.2.4); one large release makes the change abrupt.

whyNot.1: Zero tolerance applies to time and cost; scope is what flexes.
whyNot.2: Project assurance monitors governance; it does not approve release frequency.
whyNot.3: Stage boundaries still happen whatever the release pattern.

C.q: A project manager plans to use the team retrospective halfway through an iteration to check progress. What is wrong with this?
options: Retrospectives are run by the project board rather than the team
Retrospectives are held at the end of an iteration, to improve
Retrospectives happen once, in the closing a project process
Retrospectives replace the team dashboard for the iteration
C.why: Retrospectives occur at the end of an iteration and give opportunities to learn lessons and improve change adoption; they do not track progress during it (book 4.2.4).

whyNot.0: Team retrospectives are run by the team, typically facilitated by the team coach.
whyNot.2: Retrospectives happen every iteration, and project retrospectives also occur during stages.
whyNot.3: Retrospectives do not replace the team dashboard, which shows progress.

reteach.title: Learning to swim
reteach.question: Would you teach a child to swim by throwing them in the deep end on day one, or a little at a time with someone beside them?

blocks.body: Children learn to swim in the shallow end first, with an instructor watching, praising and adjusting. Each lesson builds on the last. Agile delivery treats organizational change the same way: small releases people can absorb, a user beside the team, tests and demos to react to, and regular reflection on what to do better next time.

blocks.text: A retrospective is the chat after the lesson about how to teach better next time; it is not a stopwatch during the swim.

explain.body: Frequent releases allow incremental and smooth adoption of change: users take in a little at a time rather than everything at once.

test.q: Frequent releases support OCM by allowing:
options: incremental and smooth adoption of change
the project board to skip stage boundaries
time tolerance to be widened each release
testing to be removed from each iteration
test.why: Frequent releases allow for incremental and smooth adoption of change (book 4.2.4).

whyNot.1: Stage boundaries remain whatever the release frequency.
whyNot.2: Time is fixed with zero tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile.
whyNot.3: Testing stays, and frequent testing is itself an OCM enabler.

explain.body: User representation in the delivery team facilitates organizational adoption, and frequent testing increases user engagement.

options: fixing the scope of each release
increasing user engagement
replacing the product owner
setting the cost tolerance

whyNot.0: Scope flexes in PRINCE2 Agile; testing does not fix it.
whyNot.3: Cost tolerance is set through governance, with zero tolerance for extra cost.

explain.body: Progress reviews, including demos of working products, enable user engagement and improve the speed of adoption.

test.q: Which OCM effect do progress reviews with demos have?
options: Lower time tolerance for each stage
Fewer user stories left in the product backlog
Faster adoption through user engagement
A shorter project initiation document
test.why: Progress reviews including demos enable user engagement and improve the speed of adoption (book 4.2.4).

whyNot.0: Tolerances are set through governance, not by demos.
whyNot.1: Demos may add or reorder stories; reducing them is not the stated effect.
whyNot.3: The PID is assembled in initiation; demos do not shorten it.

explain.body: Retrospectives give chances to learn lessons and act on them to improve adoption. Regular feedback can be built in during iterations and after a release.

test.q: When can regular feedback be incorporated in an agile project?
options: At project closure, once products are accepted
At stage boundaries, once the board approves
During iterations and after a release
In initiation, before any products exist
test.why: Regular feedback can be incorporated both during iterations and after a release (book 4.2.4).

whyNot.0: Waiting until closure wastes the chance to act on feedback.
whyNot.1: Feedback does not wait for board approval at boundaries.
whyNot.3: Feedback on products needs products to react to.
